newsitem.title: INDIA: Saudi airline blames Kazakh for India collision.
newsitem.headline: Saudi airline blames Kazakh for India collision.

text.p: Saudi Arabia Airlines has blamed Kazakh Airlines for a mid-air collision between their aircraft over India but the Kazakh firm blamed traffic control, lawyers said on Wednesday.
The Saudi airline, representing itself in a probe into the disaster, said the Kazakh airliner had descended below its assigned height, its lawyer Lalit Bhasin told Reuters.
It also said that modern equipment at the Delhi airport could have averted the catastrophe,
Kazakh Airlines' lawyer Duli Chand Singhania said the accident occurred due to "some serious defaults" by air traffic control.

The claims were made in a court probe into the collision last November 12 between a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Airlines Ilyushin Il-76 near Delhi in the world's worst mid-air collision. All 349 on board the aircraft were killed.
Bhasin, who made his submission to the court on Wednesday, said the Kazakh airliner descended below its assigned level of 15,000 feet (4,615 metres), causing the accident.

Bhasin said from decoding of the flight recorders at Britain's Air Accident Investigation Branch and the Aviation Institute at Moscow respectively, "it is clearly established that the Kazakh airliner had come from 15,000 feet to 14,000 feet (4,308 metres)."
"Nothing was wrong with Saudia's crew or altitude," he added.
Singhania said air traffic control informed the Kazakh airline too late that the Saudi aircraft was on the same path -- just 38 seconds before the collision.
"By the time we came to know of Saudi plane, the time was so less that no corrective measures could be taken," he said.
Both the British and Russian findings indicated air turbulence, which could have caused the Kazakh plane to fall and might have caused the accident, Singhania said.

Both lawyers said the Airport Authority of India, representing the air traffic control, said traffic control had assigned a corridor of 15,000 feet to the Kazakh airliner and 14,000 feet to the Saudi plane. The authority said the crash would not have taken place if both had stuck to their corridors.
Bhasin said the accident should not be regarded as an isolated case and that a comprehensive view of air traffic was necessary.
"This accident could have been averted if the secondary radar equipment lying at the Delhi airport for so many months had been installed," Bhasin said.
Indian aviation officials say a multi-million dollar plan to modernise radar and communications systems at major airports has fallen well behind schedule.

The installation of a state-of-the-art air traffic control system built by the U.S. Raytheon Company has been held up by technical problems. Raytheon said last November it would be ready for use soon.
